newsitem.title: JAPAN: Wheat - Japan considering buying Argentine crop.
newsitem.headline: Wheat - Japan considering buying Argentine crop.

text.p: Japan, one of the world's largest wheat importers, said on Friday it is considering buying wheat from Argentina for the first time in 22 years in an attempt to diversify its supply sources.

Japan's wheat imports in 1995 totalled nearly 5.97 million tonnes, Finance Ministry data shows. Of that, 3.28 million came from the United States, 1.56 million from Canada and 1.12 million from Australia.
"Argentina recently approached us and asked if Japan was interested in buying Argentine wheat," the Food Agency's trade division director Shinichi Yahagi told Reuters.

"We're going to receive some samples of Argentine wheat soon. And if local end-users are satisfied with the quality, we'll buy," Yahagi said. But he did not reveal when and in what amounts Japan might buy.
The Food Agency, the grain trading arm of the Agriculture Ministry, is Japan's sole importer of wheat, barley and rice and carries out weekly import tenders every Thursday.
Until 1974, Japan imported wheat from suppliers such as the former Soviet Union and Argentina.
The Food Agency said the crop quality and freight cost will be keys to determining Japanese demand for Argentine wheat.
"Domestic flour mills are very sensitive to the crop's quality. Wheat from the United States, Canada and Australia is well-known here for its stable quality," Yahagi said.
Local traders said falling prices of Argentine wheat, following its ample harvests, are prompting the agency to look at the South American crop.
In its World Supply and Demand Report released on December 12, the USDA pegged Argentina 1996/97 wheat output at 15.50 million tonnes, up from its previous estimate of 14.50 million.
The USDA also estimated Argentine 1996/97 wheat exports at 11.0 million tonnes, up from previous forecast at 10.0 million.
"Argentine wheat now looks cheaper than the American crop, and it makes sense to consider buying it," a grain trader at a major trade house in Tokyo said.
Some traders said that traditional wheat suppliers, in particular the United States, would voice their frustration if the Food Agency buys from Argentina.

"Since the end of the Second World War, the United States was mainly responsible for promoting wheat demand in Japan," a grain trader said. "As more Japanese tended to be attracted by the American lifestyle, bread consumption here has accelerated."
